##Data structure/Dataset Overview : 
The dataset contains demographic, eating habit, and physical condition variables used to classify obesity levels. Before training the ANN, the structure and quality of the dataset were inspected.

```{r}
dim(data)
head(data)
str(data)
summary(data)
```

The dataset contains both numerical and categorical variables, requiring preprocessing before ANN training.

```{r}
sum(is.na(data))
```

No missing values were present in the dataset.

##Data preprocessing for the ANN

Categorical variables were converted into factors. The target variable was then separated from the predictors: `X` contains the explanatory variables and `y` contains the obesity class to predict.

```{r}
cat_cols <- c("Gender", "family_history_with_overweight", "FAVC",
              "CAEC", "SMOKE", "SCC", "CALC", "MTRANS")

data[cat_cols] <- lapply(data[cat_cols], factor)

X <- data %>% select(-NObeyesdad)
y <- data$NObeyesdad
```

The dataset was split into training and test sets using an 80/20 ratio. The test set was kept aside and used only for the final evaluation of the ANN.

```{r}
set.seed(2)

trainIndex <- createDataPartition(y, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)

X_train <- X[trainIndex, ]
X_test  <- X[-trainIndex, ]

y_train <- y[trainIndex]
y_test  <- y[-trainIndex]
```

Since ANN models require numerical inputs, categorical predictors were transformed using one-hot encoding. Numerical features were then centered and scaled because neural networks are sensitive to feature scale.

```{r}
# One-hot encoding of predictors
dummies <- dummyVars(~ ., data = X_train)

X_train <- predict(dummies, newdata = X_train)
X_test  <- predict(dummies, newdata = X_test)

X_train <- as.data.frame(X_train)
X_test  <- as.data.frame(X_test)

# Scaling
preproc <- preProcess(X_train, method = c("center", "scale"))

X_train <- predict(preproc, X_train)
X_test  <- predict(preproc, X_test)
```

The target variable was converted into numerical classes and then one-hot encoded. This format is required for multiclass classification with a Softmax output layer and categorical cross-entropy loss.

```{r}
# Convert target to factors
y_train <- as.factor(y_train)
y_test  <- as.factor(y_test)

# Keep the same class levels in train and test
y_test <- factor(y_test, levels = levels(y_train))

# Convert classes to numbers: 0, 1, 2, ...
y_train_num <- as.numeric(y_train) - 1
y_test_num  <- as.numeric(y_test) - 1

# One-hot encoding of the target
y_train_cat <- keras::to_categorical(
  y_train_num,
  num_classes = length(levels(y_train))
)

y_test_cat <- keras::to_categorical(
  y_test_num,
  num_classes = length(levels(y_train))
)

# Convert data to matrices/arrays for Keras
X_train_matrix <- as.matrix(X_train)
X_test_matrix  <- as.matrix(X_test)

y_train_cat <- as.array(y_train_cat)
y_test_cat  <- as.array(y_test_cat)

dim(y_train_cat)
dim(y_test_cat)
head(y_train_cat)
```
## Building the Artificial Neural Network (ANN)

In this part, an Artificial Neural Network was built using the Keras and TensorFlow libraries.
The goal of the model is to learn the relationship between eating habits, physical activity, and physical characteristics in order to predict the obesity category of an individual.

The ANN used in this project is composed of:

* an input layer receiving all preprocessed variables,
* two hidden dense layers using the ReLU activation function,
* and a final Softmax output layer adapted for multiclass classification.

A relatively small architecture was chosen in order to reduce the risk of overfitting while still allowing the ANN to learn complex relationships in the data.

```{r}
# Reproducibility
set.seed(2)
tensorflow::tf$random$set_seed(2)

# Number of input features and output classes
n_features <- ncol(X_train_matrix)
n_classes <- ncol(y_train_cat)

# Build the ANN model
model <- keras_model_sequential()
model$add(layer_input(shape = n_features))
model$add(layer_dense( units = 32, activation = "relu"))
model$add(layer_dense(units = 16,activation = "relu"))
model$add(layer_dense( units = n_classes,    activation = "softmax" ))

# Display model architecture
model$summary()
```

Configuring the ANN Training

Before training the network, it is necessary to define:
* the loss function,
* the optimizer,
* and the evaluation metric.

Since this project is a multiclass classification problem, the categorical cross-entropy loss was used.
The Adam optimizer was selected because it generally provides fast and stable convergence for neural networks. Accuracy was used as the main evaluation metric during training.

```{r}
model$compile(
  loss = "categorical_crossentropy",
  optimizer = "adam",
  metrics = list("accuracy")
)
```

Training the Model

The ANN was trained on the training dataset for 100 epochs using batches of 32 observations.
A validation subset was automatically extracted from the training set (20%) in order to monitor the evolution of the model during learning and identify possible overfitting.

```{r}
history <- model$fit(
  x = X_train_matrix,
  y = y_train_cat,
  epochs = as.integer(100),
  batch_size = as.integer(32),
  validation_split = 0.2
)
```

## Evaluating the ANN Performance

After training the model, its performance was evaluated on the independent test set.
This step is important because the test data were never used during training, allowing us to estimate how well the ANN generalizes to new unseen observations.

The evaluation was performed using:

* the test accuracy,
* predicted class probabilities,
* and a confusion matrix comparing predicted and true obesity classes.

```{r}
# Evaluate the model on the test set
score <- model$evaluate(X_test_matrix, y_test_cat) ; score
```

The ANN achieved a test accuracy of approximately 91.9%, indicating that the model was able to correctly classify most individuals in the independent test set.

The relatively low loss value also suggests that the predicted class probabilities were generally close to the true obesity categories.

Overall, these results indicate that the ANN successfully learned meaningful relationships between lifestyle variables and obesity levels.

Generating Predictions

The ANN outputs probabilities for each obesity class.
The class with the highest predicted probability was selected as the final prediction for each individual.
```{r}
# Predict probabilities for each class
pred_prob <- model$predict(X_test_matrix)

# Convert probabilities into predicted class indices
pred_class_num <- max.col(pred_prob) - 1

# Recover class names
class_names <- levels(y_train)

# Convert predictions into factors
pred_class <- factor(
  class_names[pred_class_num + 1],
  levels = class_names
)

# True classes
true_class <- factor(
  y_test,
  levels = class_names
)
```

Confusion Matrix

Finally, a confusion matrix was computed in order to visualize the classification performance of the ANN for each obesity category.
This matrix allows us to identify:
* correctly classified observations,
* misclassified categories,
* and obesity classes that are more difficult for the ANN to distinguish.

```{r}
confusionMatrix(pred_class, true_class)
```

Most obesity categories were classified correctly, especially Obesity Type III, which achieved very high sensitivity and specificity values.

Most prediction errors occurred between neighboring categories such as:

- Normal Weight and Overweight Level I/Insufficient Weight,
- Overweight Level I and Overweight Level II,
- or Obesity Type I and Obesity Type II.

This behavior is expected since adjacent obesity classes often share similar physical and lifestyle characteristics.
A few less expected misclassifications were also observed. This may reflect the complexity and variability of individual lifestyle and physical condition profiles.

## Training vs Validation Loss

```{r}
plot(
  history$history$loss,
  type = "l",
  col = "blue",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Epoch",
  ylab = "Loss",
  main = "Training vs Validation Loss"
)

lines(
  history$history$val_loss,
  col = "red",
  lwd = 2
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Train Loss", "Validation Loss"),
  col = c("blue", "red"),
  lwd = 2
)  
```

The training and validation loss curves decreased progressively throughout training and remained close to each other. This suggests that the ANN converged properly and did not exhibit severe overfitting. 

## Testing an another ANN achitecture

To investigate the influence of ANN architecture on performance, a second simpler model using only one hidden layer with 16 neurons was also tested.

```{r}
model2 <- keras_model_sequential()

model2$add(layer_input(shape = n_features))

model2$add(layer_dense(units = 16,activation = "relu"))

model2$add(layer_dense(units = n_classes,activation = "softmax"))

model2$compile(loss = "categorical_crossentropy", optimizer = "adam", metrics = list("accuracy"))

history2 <- model2$fit(x = X_train_matrix, y = y_train_cat,
  epochs = as.integer(100),
  batch_size = as.integer(32),
  validation_split = 0.2,
  verbose = 0
)

score2 <- model2$evaluate(
  X_test_matrix,
  y_test_cat,
  verbose = 0
)

score2
```

Both architectures produced similar results, suggesting that the dataset can already be classified efficiently using a relatively simple ANN.
